content: In chemistry, a metal is defined as an element that easily loses electrons to form positive ions, known as cations, and forms metallic bonds between metal atoms. Metals can also form ionic bonds with non-metals. They are often described as a lattice of positive ions surrounded by a cloud of delocalized electrons. Metals are one of the three main groups of elements, alongside metalloids and nonmetals, and are distinguished by their ionization and bonding properties. On the periodic table, a diagonal line from boron (B) to polonium (Po) separates metals from nonmetals. Elements along this line are typically metalloids, also referred to as semi-metals. Elements to the lower left of this line are metals, while those to the upper right are nonmetals. An alternative definition of metals is based on their electronic structure, where they exhibit overlapping conduction and valence bands. This definition extends the category to include metallic polymers and other organic metals, which have been synthesized by researchers and are used in advanced technological devices. These synthetic materials often display the characteristic silvery-gray reflectiveness, or luster, of elemental metals. Traditional definitions of metals focus on their bulk properties, such as being lustrous, ductile, malleable, and good conductors of electricity. In contrast, nonmetals are generally brittle (if solid), lack luster, and are insulators. Chemical Properties Most metals are chemically reactive and tend to react with oxygen in the air to form oxides over varying timescales. For example, iron rusts over years, while potassium burns within seconds. Alkali metals are the most reactive, followed by alkaline earth metals, which are located in the two leftmost groups of the periodic table. Transition metals, such as iron, copper, zinc, and nickel, oxidize much more slowly. Some metals, like palladium, platinum, and gold, do not react with the atmosphere at all. Certain metals, such as aluminum, some steels, and titanium, form a protective oxide layer on their surface, which prevents further oxidation and allows them to retain their shiny appearance and conductivity for decades. Metal oxides are generally basic, unlike the acidic oxides of nonmetals, though this is more of a general rule than a strict fact. Methods such as painting, anodizing, or plating can prevent metal corrosion. However, if the coating is expected to chip, a more reactive metal in the electrochemical series should be chosen for coating. Otherwise, the coating may inadvertently promote corrosion. Physical Properties Metals are traditionally characterized by their physical properties, including metallic luster, high density, ductility, malleability, high melting points, and hardness. They are typically solid at room temperature and are excellent conductors of electricity, heat, and sound. While some metals, such as alkali and alkaline earth metals, have low density, are soft, and have low melting points, these metals are highly reactive and are rarely encountered in their pure metallic form. The electrical and thermal conductivity of metals arises from the nearly free movement of outer electrons in the metallic bond, forming an electron gas within a background of positively charged ion cores. The free electron model can mathematically predict electrical conductivity and the contribution of electrons to heat capacity and thermal conductivity, though it does not account for the detailed structure of the ion lattice. When considering the exact band structure and binding energy of a metal, the periodic arrangement of ion cores in crystals must be taken into account. This periodic potential leads to the formation of a small band gap at the boundary of the Brillouin zone, as described by the nearly-free electron model. Alloys An alloy is a solid solution composed of two or more elements, with the primary component being a metal. Pure metals are often too soft, brittle, or chemically reactive for practical use. By combining metals in different ratios to form alloys, their properties can be modified to achieve desirable characteristics. The goal of alloying is typically to make the material less brittle, harder, more resistant to corrosion, or to enhance its color and luster. Examples of alloys include steel (iron and carbon), brass (copper and zinc), bronze (copper and tin), and duralumin (aluminum and copper). Alloys designed for demanding applications, such as jet engines, may contain more than ten elements. Categories of Metals Base Metals In chemistry, the term base metal refers to a metal that oxidizes or corrodes relatively easily and reacts variably with dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl) to produce hydrogen gas. Examples include iron, nickel, lead, and zinc. Copper is also considered a base metal because it oxidizes relatively easily, although it does not react with HCl. The term is often used in contrast to noble metal. Historically, in alchemy, base metals were common and inexpensive metals, as opposed to precious metals like gold and silver. Alchemists sought to transmute base metals into precious metals. In numismatics, coins were traditionally valued based on their precious metal content, but most modern currencies are fiat currencies, allowing coins to be made from base metals. Ferrous Metals The term ferrous is derived from the Latin word for containing iron. Ferrous metals include pure iron, such as wrought iron, and iron alloys like steel. These metals are often magnetic, though not exclusively. Noble Metals Noble metals are resistant to corrosion and oxidation, unlike most base metals. They are often considered precious metals due to their perceived rarity. Examples include tantalum, gold, platinum, and rhodium. Precious Metals Precious metals are rare metallic elements with high economic value. Chemically, they are less reactive than most elements, have high luster, and exhibit excellent electrical conductivity. Historically, precious metals were important as currency but are now primarily regarded as investments and industrial commodities. Gold, silver, platinum, and palladium each have ISO 4217 currency codes. Gold and silver are the best-known precious metals, valued for their use in art, jewelry, and coinage. Other precious metals include the platinum group metals: ruthenium, rhodium, palladium, osmium, iridium, and platinum, with platinum being the most widely traded. Plutonium and uranium may also be considered precious metals. The demand for precious metals is driven not only by their practical uses but also by their role as investments and stores of value. Extraction Metals are typically extracted from the Earth through mining, which yields ores that are rich sources of the desired elements. Ores are located using prospecting techniques, followed by exploration and examination of deposits. Mineral sources are generally divided into surface mines, which are excavated using heavy equipment, and subsurface mines. Once the ore is mined, the metals must be extracted, usually through chemical or electrolytic reduction. Pyrometallurgy uses high temperatures to convert ore into raw metals, while hydrometallurgy employs aqueous chemistry for the same purpose. The methods used depend on the specific metal and its contaminants. Metallurgy Metallurgy is a branch of materials science that studies the physical and chemical behavior of metallic elements, their intermetallic compounds, and their mixtures, known as alloys. Applications Some metals and metal alloys possess high structural strength relative to their mass, making them ideal for carrying large loads or resisting impact damage. Metal alloys can be engineered to have high resistance to shear, torque, and deformation. However, metals can also be vulnerable to fatigue damage from repeated use or sudden stress failure when their load capacity is exceeded. The strength and resilience of metals have made them essential in high-rise building and bridge construction, as well as in vehicles, appliances, tools, pipes, non-illuminated signs, and railroad tracks. Metals are excellent conductors, making them valuable in electrical appliances and for transmitting electric currents over long distances with minimal energy loss. Electrical power grids rely on metal cables for electricity distribution, and home electrical systems are typically wired with copper due to its excellent conductivity. The thermal conductivity of metals is useful for containers that heat materials over a flame and for heat sinks that protect sensitive equipment from overheating. The high reflectivity of some metals is important in constructing mirrors, including precision astronomical instruments, and also makes metallic jewelry aesthetically appealing. Some metals have specialized uses; for example, radioactive metals like uranium and plutonium are used in nuclear power plants to generate energy through nuclear fission. Mercury, a liquid at room temperature, is used in switches to complete circuits when it flows over switch contacts. Shape memory alloys are used in applications such as pipes, fasteners, and vascular stents. Astronomy In astronomy and astrophysics, the term metal is used to refer to any element other than hydrogen or helium, including chemically non-metallic substances like neon, fluorine, and oxygen. Nearly all the hydrogen and helium in the universe were created during Big Bang nucleosynthesis, while all other metals were produced through nucleosynthesis in stars or supernovae. The Sun and the Milky Way Galaxy are composed of approximately 70% hydrogen, 30% helium, and 2% metals by mass.
